newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open higher on dollar gains.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open higher on dollar gains.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened higher on Wednesday, helped by a strong dollar.
"It's the dollar; it's as simple as that," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds.
The dollar continued its overnight rally in early dealings, touching 1.60 marks, its highest level since July 1994, and holding above 117 yen, near a fresh 46-month high.
The benchmark 30-year bond, meanwhile, extended Tuesday's rally, rising 4/32 to 96-21/32 to yield 6.76 percent.
"The dollar has done better and that has helped sentiment," said James Blumenthal, economist at MCM Moneywatch.

"We're continuing Tuesday's rally," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at MMS International. "There's a little bit more short-covering, European bond markets are a bit firmer and the dollar is higher."
Analysts said the lack of headline-grabbing new economic data on Wednesday's calendar could mean that the Treasury market will continue to take its cues from other trends, such as foreign exchange.
After rallying on the core December Consumer Price Index (CPI) on Tuesday, the only data the market expects today are November business inventory figures.
Economists polled by Reuters expect those to be up 0.3 percent after a 0.5 percent October increase.
"We only get business inventories," said Rupert. "I don't think those will do much for the market. It's from November so it's fairly dated and a lot of components are already known."
"Inventories are probably not going to have a major impact," said Blumenthal.

The market rallied on Tuesday after the government reported that its core December Consumer Price Index (CPI) the the CPI without its more erratic food and energy components, rose just a slight 0.1 percent, a smaller increase than the 0.2 percent gain economists and the markets had anticipated.
Rupert questioned how much farther the rally could continue on Wednesday.
"A lot of the market rally was on short-covering," she said. "As that dries up, it's a question how much further the market can go. So it's probably a trading range today."
Rupert cited resistance at 111-19/21 on the March T-bond contract and support at 111-12 and then 111-05.
Blumenthal said the U.S. Treasury market is also gaining in sympathy with European bond markets, "which have done much better this morning."

Another consideration that will start to creep into the market this afternoon is supply. The Treasury is scheduled to announce terms of its next set of monthly two- and five-year note auctions this afternoon.
"The auctions aren't until next week, but supply will become more of a factor with these auctions," Blumenthal said.
In early trade, two-year notes were unchanged at 99-19/32, yielding 5.97 percent.
Three- and six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.03 percent and 5.08 percent, respectively. Year bill rates were up one basis point to 5.30 percent.
Five-year notes were unchanged at 99-9/32, yielding 6.30 percent. Ten-year notes were down 1/32 to 99-27/32, yielding 6.52 percent.
